text: We're going to go ahead and get started. Welcome everyone to our September 19, 2023 Budget Committee meeting, and everyone should have a copy of the agenda in front of you. We have only two items to go over today, and one is the FY 2023 carryover review, followed by an update on the opioid settlements.

And so to get us started, I am going to turn over to Phil Hagan, who is the Director of department of management and budget to begin the carryover presentation welcome thank you and so katie horseman my deputy director we're going to tag team this joe lahate our other deputy director is and christina jackson are also here to help out if we get to questions at the end so fy 2023 carryover we can start on slide two where we're looking at the remaining balances as of year end fy 2023 and our recommendations for allocations of those balances so within the

general fund we ended the year with 203 million dollars in balance and just the the high level summary before we get into the detailed slides first our FY 2023 commitments total 70 million dollars this primarily includes outstanding encumbrances as well as re-appropriation of the 12 million dollar general fund pandemic reserve as well as the balance in the hiring incentive program reserve which is just a little over two million dollars then we have our allocations for reserves and capital, really just capital at this point, combined 50% of the balance

going towards the capital sinking fund as well as bike and pedestrian projects, totaling $69 million, including the reserve impact. And then we have other requirements, which will be the bulk of this presentation, totaling $60 million. As is typical with our carryover review, we're looking primarily at capital and IT projects for those funds, as well as our environmental and energy strategies and support for our park system.
So all told, our staff recommendations for the carryover balances total just under $201 million, leaving a net general fund balance of $2.24 million. The-- oh, we have a font issue.

OK, I apologize for that. So the right-hand column then talking about our ARPA coronavirus state and local recovery funds, where we ended the year with $118.7 million remaining to be spent and Katie will detail that in a couple slides and so we are recommending carryover of those balances so that we're able to spend them in the new year.

So moving on to slide three, allocations for reserves and for capital. So we have three different policies in place that are the kind of across the top, the first cuts at our balances from carryover. The first being allocating 40% of our year in balances to reserves as has been the case for the past couple of years, we ended the year with our reserves at their target of 10%.

And so, once again, we do not need to take that first cut for reserves. I would note that we have included reserve loadings on all the adjustments that are included in this package to keep us at the 10% target. So, all told, we have $8.76 million going towards reserves as part of this package.

The next cut, though, is 30% of the balance targeted towards the capital sinking fund. That totals $39.7 million. Allocating that is out to agencies, $18 million of that to facilities management, $10 million for schools, $6 million for parks, and the remainder for walkways, roads, and revitalization.

And then the third allocation, 20% of the balance, or $26.5 million, is allocated to support bicycle and pedestrian projects. This, combined with the $30 million that's previously been put towards those projects, we now have reached $56.7 million of the $100 million goal.

towards those projects Okay, like Phil said, I'm just going to give a brief update on where we are with our stimulus funding So we have recommended a full allocation of our ARPA fiscal recovery funds We did send a memo to the board on Friday on any of those allocation updates So in total just as a reminder we received two hundred and twenty two million dollars in ARPA funding And we allocated more than half of that
to individuals, small businesses, nonprofits, to aid them in their recovery from the pandemic. And then we also should note that we allocated $55 million to affordable housing initiatives.

So that's about 25% of the total $222 million allocation, so a significant portion. In order to continue the projects, we do need to reappropriate our balance. like phil said we have 118.71 million left unspent that needs to be reappropriated as part of carryover right now we need to obligate by december of 2024 the full arpa allocation and then we have until december of 2026 to actually spend the arpa allocation moving on to our fema reimbursements

so fema is reimbursed so as costs are incurred we request them for the federal government to pay us back. So at this point, we have submitted all of our reimbursement requests related to our response to the pandemic. Those total just over $104 million. And if you remember, FEMA, typically there's a cost share associated with it. At the start of the pandemic, that cost share was waived. So the federal government's been reimbursing us at 100%. But beginning in July of 2022, federal government and shifted that cost share to 90% federal and 10% county.

So we do have some expenses where there will be a county match, but that's we're estimating about just under $500,000. And we have included an allocation in ARPA to account for that $500,000 that we're expecting.

And then finally on here, we have the balance of our general fund pandemic reserve. We do have just over $12 million left in this reserve. It is largely available to either supplement our current stimulus projects and/or for other county priorities and initiatives.

We do have one outstanding housing project that we're still working on. We also do recommend leaving a small balance there just in case there's any unforeseen needs in human services throughout this fiscal year. But again, there is a large balance there that's available for other priorities and initiatives at this time.

Just a quick question, Katie, before we move on. Can you remind us what the peak amount was in that account? Right now the balance is $12.04 million, but what was it at its highest point? $22 million. I mean, when we first started, $22 million. Okay, so roughly about a little over half of it is available.

Yes. Okay, thank you. So now moving on, looking at those other allocations within the carryover package, we're starting off with some of the board priorities. And as we have done in recent carrier packages, a significant amount of funding going to our environmental and energy strategies, $8 million in this package.

Just some of the highlights, $3 million is included for building energy improvements. And then we also have $1.8 million for the final year of the LED streetlight conversion program. At this point, 36,000 of the 56,000 streetlights have been converted.

$1.4 million for solar panel installations at some county facilities, and $1 million for some energy improvements at park authority facilities, including building automation, HVAC, lighting, and bathroom upgrades. We've also included $1 million, $100,000 for each board office for small-scale capital projects in their supervisor districts, and then also a little over half a million dollars in adjustments that are consistent with board action as part of the third quarter review.

$300,000 to improve library collections. I understand Paw Patrol is top on their list. And then $230,000 for the illegal sign removal program. Partial year funding was put in as part of third quarter, and so this completes the full year funding.

We have a number of adjustments supporting the park authority. All told in this package, park authority funding totals $15.7 million. $5 million is included for some of the cost escalations that they're experiencing with their capital projects. This is consistent with the actions that we took last carryover as well as this last third quarter to continue to supplement the park authority funds.

$2.5 million is included for turf field replacements. $740,000 for some of the park's capital equipment. $500,000 to continue to support the forestry operations division. And then these last two are included in the totals on previous slides.

$6 million is their allocation out of the capital sinking fund and $1 million for energy improvements. And, of course, we also continue to find ways to support parks outside of the annual budget process. As part of the stimulus memo that went out late last week, we've recommended an additional $7.5 million towards park maintenance out of the ARPA funds.

That's the second tranche of $7.5 million for now a total of $15 million in ARPA funds going to support their maintenance. And then significant investments in our capital program overall, $7 million, supporting improvements at the workhouse campus.

This is primarily some of the structural repairs at buildings 13 and 15, which are being renovated for new tenants. There's also some initial work assessments, as well as some remediation at four of the unoccupied buildings, and then paving and lighting throughout the site. $5 million is included for our construction escalation reserve.

We certainly continue to see rising costs across all of our capital projects as they go out to bid, and so this has been very helpful to help us deal with some of those cost overruns. $5 million included for emergency systems failures. That's for major system failures such as HVAC and roofs.

$3 million for space realignment. We continue to try to find ways to reduce agency footprints, hoping for some long-term efficiencies and savings, especially getting us out of some of our leased space. $3,000,000 to temporarily relocate the clinical services that are currently at the Willard Health Center so that that facility can be renovated.

And then also $800,000 for some security assessments and improvements at county facilities, including at board offices. Also, substantial investments in IT, continuing our trend here as well to invest in IT infrastructure as part of our third quarter in carryover reviews.

all told $14.5 million. The largest adjustment here is our third tranche of investing in the replacement of voting machines. We previously invested $5 million as part of the last carryover and then $5 million as this past third quarter. And so this gets us through this round of replacement of those voting machines. And then $9.5 million for various other projects. And I won't go through that list just out of. Okay, so we wanted to spend a little bit of time on our expansion of youth mental health services. If you remember, as part of the budget guidance that was

passed this past spring, staff were directed to develop a recommendation to have a more robust mental health system, specifically focusing on youth and adolescents. So the CSB has come back and provided three different options. We'll get into some more detail on the next slide, but those three options included medication-assisted treatment, youth mental health outreach, engagement, and intervention services, and then the last option was the youth crisis services and re-entry program. So the options provided by CSB, we do want to note that they do address both mental

health and substance use disorders, since those are often co-occurring disorders, and about 50% of the youth will, if they have a mental health challenge, they will have a substance use disorder challenge. So they do address both of those components. The three options also complement each other. So it's not like we have to implement medication assisted treatment followed by the youth mental health outreach followed by youth crisis.

So they complement each other but they can be implemented independent of each other. So then over on slide number 10 is just looking at a little bit more detail on each of those three different options and then our proposed path forward with each one. So first one again is our medication assisted treatment. So this is a combination of counseling and behavioral therapies and it's really focusing on substance use disorders and the opioid overdose and preventing those overdoses. We did not include any funding in this carryover package for

option number one. We think that this would probably be a good use with our opioid settlement funds and Ellen as we know is going to give a presentation following this one on where where she is with that process. Option number two is our youth mental health outreach engagement intervention services. So this is establishing three teams of healthcare professionals working in targeted areas of the county to increase capacity for the youth mental health services each team will be able to serve 300 youth each year so that's a

total of 900 youth annually it does include an additional 18 merit positions so this budget recommendation does include the additional 18 positions and our program expenses of just under 3 million CSV does have some balances this year that they'll be able to use those balances as well as some revenue so the program will generate revenue. At this point, it's hard to know how much revenue it will generate since it is a new program and we're just getting it up and running. But there will be revenue to offset these expenses as well. So all that being said, we don't need any new resources in 2024.

We just need the 18 positions in order to move forward with this option. And then lastly, we have option number three, which is a youth crisis services and re-entry program. So this is really a dedicated youth crisis facility with the goal of re-entry back into the community for these youth. So this is a longer-term proposal. We did not include any funding since it is a longer-term proposal. The idea would be that CSB either leased or buy a facility. They did have some one-time balances totaling $15 million that we were able to set aside for this initiative. The

recommendation at carryover does not include any operating expenses since it is a longer-term project. But at some point, we will need to come back and add those operating expenses in any additional positions if they were needed at that point. So the carryover package does recommend 32 new positions. 18 of those are within the CSB, as Katie just described, and those would be supported by revenue as well as existing CSB balances, at least in the near term. We are recommending as well eight positions and land development services to help with

their customer technical support center continuing to deal with the call volume there with land development services now being a separate fund those positions would be supported by revenues within that fund and then we have six positions that are recommended that are associated with workload requirements for collective bargaining those include two positions in the Department of Human Resources two in DMV and two in the County Attorney's Office those requiring general fund support of 0.87 million partial year impact and 1.24 million dollars recurring. So we do have currently 10 consideration items that have been

submitted by the board listed here. So out of our $2.24 million balance that I mentioned, there have been these total $1.9 million in allocations of that balance, as well as two adjustments that would reallocate $9 million. So we have a $500,000 consideration item that would support permanent supportive housing, $500,000 to construct ADA accessible doors and facilities at the old firehouse, a quarter of a million dollars to support the TOPS program, expanding from four to six annual subsidies per participant

per year, $200,000 for the Lake Anne Economic Visioning Project, $150,000 for the Springfield Branding Project, $125,000 to support SPARK, $100,000 for improvements at the Annandale Civic Space, $75,000 for a survey of people who are panhandling in the county, and then a reallocation of $8 million out of that $12 million balance in the General Fund Pandemic Reserve to support affordable housing, as well as a reallocation of $1 million that is currently in the package to support the Supervisor District Capital Projects to instead support the Park

Authority for tree removal and maintenance. So looking ahead of the budget calendar, closing out the carryover process will be a public hearing followed by action on carryover at the board meeting next Tuesday, September 26th. Then our staff is also in early development of the FY 2025 budget. You know, certainly not too much has changed since the picture that we painted in our

We do anticipate this to be another difficult budget year certainly some of the the talk about recession has ebbed but we do know that there's some some headwinds out there the potential for a federal government shutdown coming also the the looming needs of Metro as well as a number of other funding priorities that are out there.

So based on board budget guidance we are trying to make sure that we continue to have plenty of options on the table as we go into 2025. We have asked our agencies to do a comprehensive review of all of their user fees as well as the rates to look and see what kind of revenue options there are out there.

We also are asking agencies to come up with those agencies that receive general fund support to come up with reduction options totaling 7% of that support so that we are able to look, primarily trying to find those places where we have efficiencies and other savings that can be taken, lessons learned from the pandemic or places where they realize perhaps based on IT development that they don't need some of the positions that have been vacant for some time.

Staff are early in reviewing those. We know that we've seen a kind of wide range of what we're getting back from agencies. We see some that are certainly common sense where we have positions that have been vacant for a while and agencies really have learned to work without them. On the other side of the range, we're certainly seeing some options come back that we don't think should be on the table.

So as we work through the FY 2025 budget process, we'll be reviewing all these options and really trying to come up with a measured approach to come up with a good package for all of you to consider. So our next touch point with you in our FY 2025 development will be the financial forecast, our joint forecast with the school board, which will be presented at the Budget Policy Committee meeting on November 28th, and then we will be presenting the county executive's advertised budget to you on February 20th.

Okay. Thank you very much for that presentation, and we're going to open it up for questions. Before we do that, I do want to thank staff for their slide on the expansion of youth mental health services. I mean, this is something that I think it started with the summertime task force that was set up after I did my board matter a couple years ago now.

It feels like it was just yesterday, and I know we've chipped away at this for the last two years, as you mentioned. I guess my only question, and I appreciate the creative use of funding, by the way. I mean, the opioid settlement funds, this is exactly, you know, what they should be being used for, for option number one.

But I guess on option number three was referred to as a longer term proposal. And with, I guess the logical question is with $15 million sitting there and a mental health crisis real time happening with our young people today, the logical question is why does that have to be part of a longer term proposal and what do we mean by longer term?

I mean, obviously, we know the logistics of trying to find space and dealing with that is one of those pieces that could be a challenge, but is this something actively being worked on, and what would we define as a longer-term proposal? Yes, so it is actively being worked on right now, longer-term being passed carryover in September, so they are looking for space.

The funding just wasn't needed in the September timeframe, so yes, they are actively looking for space right now, whether that's the leased space and or purchase. And as soon as they have something, they can come forward and we can bring it back to the board for discussion. Good. Excellent.

I appreciate that. And then my last question, I'll open up to others, is the, if I was tracking right on the park authority numbers, I know that, you know, there were a number of tranches that you mentioned there, both in this package and then also the $7.5 million ARPA funds that you mentioned in passing that also are being allocated, the $1 million from Supervisor District Capital Projects, I know Supervisor Herdy had put that on the table, was specifically for tree removal and maintenance, and I just want to be clear on this point, are any of

the funds that are already included in the carryover or related to the ARPA funds that are being transferred to the park authority, do any of them cover the same expense? So, you know, I think there's certainly a need there. There's a large need there. What we have programmed within the carryover, I'd say that would be kind of

Specific to those would be the half million dollars for forestry operations. Then certainly, as we mentioned with ARPA, that second seven and a half million dollar tranche towards maintenance. I think what would be helpful, at least to me, is I don't doubt that.

I know they have tremendous needs, would be to see what has happened with that so that we know. And so I want to make sure that the number is substantiated and that if what you just described, if you can outline for us what has happened with that. Because my fear of using one-time money for something like maintenance is it's great, it gets you caught up in a year. But then this problem comes back again next year.

So any help you can give us in understanding, you know, what has been done over the last couple of years, kind of what that hole is, if there's a hole, if there's money that's been used for other things within the park system, if there's a hole there that needs to be filled, what that amount is, I think would be helpful for us to know in considering that particular item that's on the consideration item list.

And then lastly, and I just want to get a confirmation of this, if we did not reallocate that $1 million, every supervisor could reallocate their portion of it towards that, correct? There's absolutely nothing stopping a supervisor from reallocating that amount to the park authority for that use, even if the board doesn't fully reallocate that entire account, correct?

That's correct. Okay. I just wanted to make sure, just from a fact standpoint, that that was right. That's all I have in the way of questions. Why don't we start here, especially since we were just talking about the parks item with Supervisor Harry. We'll go down and make sure everyone has a chance.

Yeah, and I met with the Park Authority, and they are $2.4 million, according to them, in the hole for tree this year. We put a little bit of money, I think, earlier this year towards trees. Primarily, McLean Civic Association did a deep kind of dive in there at their budget committee, and we did that as a result.

But the problem is they've got to do the tree. It's emergency tree removal. It's not even preventative tree removal. And then they're holding maintenance positions open so that they can pay to have emergency tree removal done. And it's creating the maintenance issues we're seeing in our parks.

So the $1 million was the one-time kind of hole that they've got this year. We do need to address the ongoing issue, and the time to do that clearly is at budget. I did take $150,000 out of my, I wish I had that to give, but I don't.

I'd give it back to the taxpayers. But $150,000 and put it into Burke Lake Park to make some much-needed capital improvements there. So I have done that. I'm going to go ahead and ask a follow-up question to your question.

At the same time, what kind of capital projects were we looking at? Does anybody have a list of – because I think there's a lot. Can we have the list of unspent funds that we have that I used for the park authority thing?

My question, my other question, so what drove that and which projects are not getting done because of the $100,000 in each supervisory district? So there's no correlation between the amount that's being asked for and the need. That's what I was trying to get at. That's what I wanted to make sure everybody understood here is that this was a number that was in the budget that was used to reallocate so that we wouldn't have to spend additional money.

but it doesn't have any relationship to what is actually needed for the Park Authority for tree removal and maintenance now. And that's what I was getting at. I think that's what I just heard you say. It gets them close to that $2.4 million, but not entirely to their $2.4 million. Between what we did earlier, this additional $0.5 million plus the million gets you pretty close to $2.4 million.

I don't know that things have changed that much from what we included in the multi-year, but I think that our multi-year overall revenue increase for all categories was about $50 million, a little over $50 million, primarily based on real estate.

Okay. All right. Thank you for that. Okay. Okay. Kathy? Okay. So I'll just go with the consideration item for the $1 million. I don't support that. I have used that funding for streetlights, one in an area where there was a lot of crime, And another one that we're using where a pedestrian was killed crossing Route 29.

So I really value that money to make a difference in my district. And I have been using that money and would like to have that replenished so I can deal with other issues. You know, I'm looking forward to the next year's budget, and I'm hoping we maybe rethink how we do some things.

I think we have a tendency not to look big picture at what we do. And probably my thinking gets so influenced by spending 14 years on the school board whenever we did have carryover. I mean, money to use, we saved it for carryover for the next budget.

And so, you know, we deal with issues or consideration items, but we don't step back and I think have a good enough knowledge about some of the big picture things we need to invest in. And so I'd like that discussion to happen into the next year's budget.

I don't have any specific questions right now. Thank you. Thank you, Kathy. Supervisor Stork? Thank you, Mr. Chairman. A couple of points and a question for Chris Leonard. I was surprised the turf field replacement for the Park Authority, it's $2.5 million.

My understanding is when we do turf fields, we put together a sinking fund. I know on the school side, that's what we did. I thought we did the same thing on the county side. Why do we need $2.5 million for that? I think it's based on the timing of some of the field replacements that right now we just have a dip.

So we just need a one-time infusion to get us through the next couple of years, and then I think we're going to be on an appropriate cycle. So I don't think there's necessarily a recurring need because we do have funds set aside for turf field replacement. It's just based on some of the timing of some of the replacements coming up, we see a little bit of a funding gap.

And so we just want to fill that gap to then put us in a good position for going forward. So the $2.5 million is kind of one time. You won't need something. You don't expect to need something. It's just based on kind of the timing of when the fields are getting replaced. The sinking funds should then work from that point forward.

Have we done something like this in the last year or two, or parks, or any? No, we have not had to put in any one-time infusion for turf field replacement in a few years, I believe. Thank you. I obviously strongly support the mental health improvements that are in here.

I am concerned because what I read and understand is that we have essentially some maybe one-time money that's being used, but then in FY 2025, we're going to need to make that, those are going to need to be ongoing dollars.

Did I misunderstand that? Not necessarily. Based on the revenue that comes in from the program, we're also hoping, you know, we were waiting for the state budget to be passed to see if there was any additional funding there that could be put towards the initiative, so not necessarily. So you're expecting Medicaid dollars and state dollars to offset the staffing that's in here for the?

That's what we're hoping, yes. And do we have any sense of how hopeful that is? Is it X percent or highly likely or reasonably likely? Or in other words, what's your internal calculation that there's a 90% likelihood that or whatever that the state and or Medicaid will pay that?

So I don't think staff wants to commit since it's a new program. They really are unsure about the revenue, the Medicaid revenue that will come in. You know, they can approximate based on adults, which is very favorable. But, you know, they don't want to say it's going to be completely covered and then have the youth be a completely different model compared to what they see on the adult side.

And then the state budget was just passed, so they're still working through that. Okay. I mean, we absolutely need more and better youth services, and I just want to understand what that commitment is that we're making. And the last item is I know some of us were provided with a memo from Mary Payton and the NAACP and South County Task Force Ventures and Community, those organizations, about the need for additional dollars, especially for rent, utility, legal relief.

And I wanted to ask Chris if he could kind of give my concern is clear cut. I don't want to run out of funds, particularly as we transition. We all know that we had a significant amount of money. We're transitioning down a little bit from that, but that transition, in my mind, should still be based upon ensuring that we have sufficient funds to fund the needs that exist not only this year, but also making sure that we don't cut our shelves short for future years.

And a couple of points that were made is we still have levels of call volumes as well as the still. And one thing that particularly concerned me, because I had not heard this before, and I had a conversation with, I would say, the housing and homeless advocates a week or so ago, and they were advising me that we absolutely do not have sufficient bed space for the folks who may need it on an emergency basis.

So if you could just wrap those together and give us your comments. And I have a follow-up question to that. Sure. Well, first, to answer the question, I do think I have to provide a little bit of context. pre-pandemic rent assistance program, about $4 million a year. Rent assistance was truly emergency rent assistance. It was only intended to be temporary. A couple of months, somebody lost their job due to injury, due to whatever, and needed a little bit of help. But certainly after a couple months, they'd be able to pick up paying the rent again. That's what the typically operated local

rent assistance was, and it's why it's kind of operated out of NCS instead of our housing community development department. The pandemic hits, we literally got tens of millions of dollars, but along with that, we got extended capabilities, both in terms of income that we could serve, but then also how much time.

So we had a number of residents that were able to be helped for 12 months, even some that could go a little bit further than that. That was not in line with anything that we would call a typical local emergency rent assistance.

But certainly, in recognition of a worldwide pandemic, we had massive job losses. People were trying to figure out ways. We serve people that didn't know what the 222 line. That was all new to them, and they haven't called since. They only needed help to get through that. And fortunately, the federal government came through with literally tens of millions.

We had $70 million only for rent assistance, and that's on top of the CARES Act, $20 million. Certainly spent close to $100 million on that. We knew last summer, we being our staff, knew that, hey, we're going to be having to transition at some point back to our local rent assistance efforts.

But we also knew that we couldn't go back to $4 million in 2023. So what we did is we went to Christina and we said, let's see if we can figure out a way to get to a bridge program. So we developed a bridge program with $4 million in our regular general fund and $10 million in ARPA to be able to do that.

What we did during that time, and I challenged our staff, I need you guys to look at what the needs are, look at what the criterias are. Was it a couple months? Is three months right? Is two months right? What is right? The entire program criteria, because we wanted to make sure in 24 we were ready for the post-pandemic rent assistance.

And our staff came back with a number of about $7.6 million. So we had $4 million that we could put to that in our general fund, $3.6 million, which is covered, again, via ARPA. I will point out for the board, it's not provided for in 2025, and there is no ARPA in 2025.

So as I've told the advocates, we don't have this capability, but that is our new rent assistance program at 7.6. I'd also be remiss to tell you that staff, in addition to need and months and all of those sorts of things and looking at what everybody else is doing, I did say we have to be reasonable looking at feasibility of funding asks.
